PCI.BIO: Dr. Choi worked at Korea Telecom Research Center as a research engineer between 1995 and 1999, where he led the design and development of a network data communication. Dr. Choi received Ph.D. degree from the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the Georgia Institute of Technology in 2005 with a title “A Three dimensional Coupled Microelectrode and Microfluidic Array for Neural Interfacing”. After he finished his PhD project with biomedical applications, he went deep into the biological area to make the solid interdisciplinary research background. While he worked at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center as a research engineer for four years, he was awarded the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society career development grant. Coming back to the original PhD work of neuroscience research, he was a research faculty in the Department of Biomedical Engineering at the Georgia Institute of Technology in 2010. Since then, he has been working on a regenerative peripheral nerve interface system as his second interdisciplinary research along with cancer research. In 2013, he joined in the Department of Electrical Engineering at UTRGV as an assistant professor and has continued his neuroscience and cancer research. He became a tenured associate professor in 2017. His research interests include Neural interfaces, Cancer, and MEMS.

PCI_RESEARCH_INTERESTS.DESC: Dr. Choi’s research interest focuses on two frontiers of neuroscience: 1) the development of the single neuron peripheral nerve interface system, and 2) the mapping of animal behavioral patterns with global neural network data throughout both the central and the peripheral nervous systems (CNS-PNS). This is attainable using a three-level single neuron network that consists of a single neuron peripheral nerve interface (SNI) placed on the peripheral nervous system and custom-designed µCuff/µECoG interfaces on the central nervous system. The SNI isolates individual axons and communicates with them. It gives us the capability of both electrophysiological recording and stimulation to complete a single neuron network (SNN) from the brain to the endings of peripheral nerves.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Equipment: MRI: Track 1 Acquisition of Polytec MSA-600 Micro System Analyzer for Biomedical Engineering
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Requested Instrument: Polytec MSA-600-X/U Micro System Analyzer ($695,790), state-of-the-art instrument crucial for biomedical engineering research and education the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). The location of the instrument is the BIO-MEMS Laboratory (Director Caruntu). Servingover 34,000 students, UTRGV is a non-PhD-granting, minority-serving institution with a predominantly Hispanic student body (92%). The university aims to become an emerging research institution and establish a strong biomedical engineering community. This advanced equipment is crucial to preparing students in engineering, science, and medicine by providing hands-on research experiences that can lead to graduate studies, academic roles, or leadership positions in industry. UTRGV is experiencing rapid growth, with increasing student enrollment and the hiring of new faculty. A recently formed Biomedical Engineering(BME) Cluster for research and education includes eight faculty members, four of whom were hired within the past two years. Supporting faculty research development depends on access to cutting-edge infrastructure like the requested analyzer. Securing this grant lays a foundation for attracting external funding and fostering multidisciplinary collaborations. The lack of this instrument currently limits research efforts. This proposal is strongly supported by UTRGV administration, aligning with the university’s strategic goal of building a robust biomedical engineering research and education program.

CONGRANT.TITLE: NSF DMREF: (Pending, $1,997,394) Multifunctional High-Performance Fiber-Reinforced Geopolymers for Smart and Sustainable Infrastructures
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Fiber-reinforced geopolymer concrete with non-structural multifunction is suggested in this proposed project as an alternative construction material that has potential to cope with pressing challenges such as climate change and deterioration of modern infrastructures. Production of high CO2 emissions and low ductility are the shortcomings of conventional Portland cement concrete. The use of geopolymer concrete can substantially reduce CO2 emissions with improved durability. However, the complex and sensitive relations between multiple factors and mechanical performance of geopolymer hinders its standardization and widespread use. On the other hand, while fiber reinforcement in concrete is known to be an effective way to engineer the desired tensile/flexural properties, its application to geopolymer concrete is in the research stage. The proposed project aims to fill the technical gaps for the practical use and standardization of high-performance fiber-reinforced geopolymer by using AI-driven machine learning models and providing basic knowledge to engineer its performance. The data on the combined effects of geopolymer ingredients, fiber reinforcement, and other factors such as aggregate and curing conditions on strength, ductility, and internal pore structures will be collected through literature review and the proposed experimental program and will be analyzed using AI-driven machine learning tools to find the multiparameter relations. The project also investigates three potential multifunctional applications – damage sensing, strain sensing, and permeable reactive barrier – using advanced measurements including electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), electrical impedance tomography (EIT), and X-ray tomography (X-ray CT).

CONGRANT.TITLE: UTRGV Seed Grant: Electrochemical Impedance Tomography for Evaluating Internal Structures of Concrete
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The objective of the proposed project is to develop a nondestructive tool for evaluating the internal structures of concrete using 3D Electrochemical Impedance Tomography (EIT). The proposed EIT will generate 3D conductivity maps of cementitious composites and is expected to identify internal flaws/cavities, rebars, and microcracks. Concrete is the second most used material after water in modern civilization, and the evaluation of internal damage is critical for structural safety. The proposed idea is that flaws and rebars alter the conductive path in concrete, and internal structural maps can be constructed by monitoring the changes in electrochemical properties. EIT for concrete is an emerging nondestructive technique combining Impedance Spectroscopy and Tomography, but the application of EIT for concrete has not been well established yet. Upon success, the EIT allows real-time safety monitoring of concrete structures, and its application can be expanded to detect other damages such as underground sink holes.
